paper_title: Omega-S: A Functional Resilience Index for LLM Fine-Tuning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Fine-tuning a large language model on new data degrades what it previously learned. We present Omega-S, a drop-in penalty computed from the weight matrix alone: it needs no previous-task data, no Fisher matrix and no stored copy of the old weights. It is three lines in an existing training loop and adds under 4% to the cost of a step. Retention. On Llama-3-8B with LoRA, fine-tuned from code to prose and measured by HumanEval over ten seeds, Omega-S retains more of the original capability than no regularisation on 9 of 10 seeds (0.173 -> 0.238 absolute pass@1; sign test one-sided p=0.011, Wilcoxon p=0.006), as a retention ratio, 62.9% -> 84.1%. It also beats tuned weight decay on 10 of 10 seeds (p=0.002) and tuned EWC on 8 of 10 (p=0.014), every arm re-measured in the same session. Mechanism, measured rather than asserted. Omega-S is topological by construction, its objective built from Tr(A^3), but we measured which of its four factors actually moves and three do not: their elasticity with respect to the weights is at or below 1e-4, against 9e-3 for the degree-variance term. As implemented, the composite reduces to a penalty on the variance of node degrees, which means row magnitude in square modules and directional alignment in non-square ones. We report this because a method whose name promises one thing and whose gradient does another should say so. We also enumerate the open design choices, including a contrast-preserving construction that does what it was designed to do and makes retention worse on all ten seeds. Repeating an identical configuration, same seed and same hardware, gives a standard deviation of 0.104 in retention ratio. We have not found this quantified for low-rank fine-tuning of language models, and it bounds every seed-paired comparison in this literature, ours included. Code, per-seed results and the full record of negative results are available.

sections.content: Omega-S: Functional Resilience Index for LLM Fine-Tuning Alberto Acedo1 1Biome Makers Inc. August 5, 2026 Abstract Fine-tuning large language model on new data degrades what it previously learned. We present Omega-S, drop-in penalty computed from the weight matrix alone: it needs no previous-task data, no Fisher matrix and no stored copy of the old weights, which is what the standard baseline for this problem requires. It is three lines in an existing training loop and adds under 4% to the cost of step. Retention. On Llama-3-8B with LoRA, fine-tuned from code to prose and measured by HumanEval over ten seeds, Omega-S leaves the model with more of its original capability than no regularisation on 9 of 10 seeds (0.173 0.238 absolute pass@1, 37.7% relative increase; exact sign test, one-sided = 0.011, Wilcoxon = 0.006). As retention ratio the same comparison gives 62.9% 84.1%. It also beats tuned weight decay on 10 of 10 seeds (p = 0.002) and tuned EWC on 8 of 10 (p = 0.014) on the same absolute measure, with every arm re-measured in the same session so that the comparison does not mix effect with run-to-run variation. The design space. Turning the index into penalty leaves three choices open: how the graph is built from the weights, which form of the objective is used, and how the modularity factor is oriented. We enumerate all three and report what each costs, including contrastpreserving construction that does what it was designed to do and makes retention worse on all ten seeds. Two of the three choices turn out not to matter for the mechanism, and we show why. Mechanism, measured rather than asserted. Omega-S is topological by construction, its objective being built from Tr(A3), but we measured which of its four factors actually moves during training and three of them do not. Their elasticity with respect to the weights is at or below 104, against 9 103 for the degree-variance term, before and after training alike; during run the degree variance falls by 5.9% in median while the other three stay under 0.1%. As implemented, the composite objective reduces in practice to penalty on the variance of node degrees, quantity that means row magnitude in square modules and directional alignment in non-square ones. An ablation shows the alignment channel leading the magnitude channel on 8 of 10 seeds. We also built the contrast-preserving reformulation that earlier drafts proposed as an open direction, and report that it makes retention worse on all ten seeds under either orientation: the inert clustering channel was not defect holding the method back. How much run-to-run variation this setting carries. Repeating an identical configuration, same seed and same hardware, gives standard deviation of 0.104 in retention ratio. We report it because we have not found it quantified for low-rank fine-tuning of language models, and because it bounds the reading of any seed-paired comparison, including ours. Two forms of the penalty exist and they are not interchangeable; they rank oppositely across the two settings above, and we define both explicitly (Section 2.1). Code, per-run results and the full record of negative results are at https://github.com/BiomeMakers/OmegaS-LLM under AGPL-3.0 for research use. 1 1. Introduction 1.1. An index from soil, and what it measures The quantity this paper minimises did not originate in machine learning. It comes from body of work on agricultural microbiomes, where the object of study is co-occurrence network of taxa and the practical question is whether soil community is functionally integrated or dominated by few organisms. survey of 350 vineyard soils across two countries [1] found that the communities associated with resistance to perturbation share signature: higher clustering, lower modularity and lower co-exclusion. Communities with the opposite signature are diverse by count and fragile in practice, because small set of organisms carries the connectivity. That signature was formalised as an index, Ω = D/(M Coex), on four measures of weighted graph: clustering C, density D, modularity measure , and concentration term Coex given by the variance of the degree sequence. The index is high when connectivity is distributed and low when it is monopolised by few nodes. Its theoretical development, including the identity Tr(A3) = (cid:80) λ3 and the conditions under which the index is comparable across graphs, is in companion manuscript [21]. 1.2. The Production Problem: Weight Monopolies Every organisation that fine-tunes large language models on proprietary data faces the same hidden cost: the model forgets. Update general-purpose model on customer support data, and it loses coding ability. Fine-tune on legal documents, and general reasoning degrades. This is catastrophic forgetting, and it means that the compute cost of fine-tuning is paid twice: once to train, and once to repair what broke. Standard regularisers do not solve this. Weight decay pushes all parameters toward zero indiscriminately. SAM optimises loss landscape curvature. Neither addresses the structural root cause: during training, small subset of neurons progressively concentrates disproportionate connectivity across layers, creating weight monopolies. When new data arrives, these monopolies are overwritten first, destroying the representations that made the model valuable. Omega-S targets weight monopolies directly. 1.3. Our Contributions regulariser from an ecological index. We define Omega-S, penalty on the connectivity graph of weight matrix, built from Tr(A3) and estimated by Hutchinsons method so that its cost is O(N 2) rather than O(N 3). It needs no previous-task data, no Fisher matrix and no stored copy of the old weights, and adds under 4% to the cost of training step. design space, mapped rather than assumed. Three choices are open in turning the index into penalty: the graph construction, the form of the objective and the orientation of the modularity factor. We screen six constructions, define both forms of the objective, and settle the orientation from the ecological observation the index formalises. The variant that looks most promising priori, contrast-preserving construction that revives the clustering term, is measured and makes retention worse on all ten seeds. Retention on Llama-3-8B. The selected variant leaves more code capability after sequential fine-tune than no regularisation on 9 of 10 seeds (0.173 0.238 absolute HumanEval, +37.7% relative, sign test = 0.011, Wilcoxon = 0.006), and beats tuned weight decay on 10 of 10 and tuned EWC on 8 of 10 on the same measure, with every arm re-measured in one session. mechanism that contradicts the name. Omega-S is topological by construction, and we measure that three of its four factors are numerically inert: elasticities at or below 104 against 2 9 103 for degree variance, before and after training alike, with the degree variance the only factor that moves during run. As implemented, the objective reduces in practice to penalty on the variance of node degrees. We report this because method whose name promises one thing and whose gradient does another should say so. How much run-to-run variation this setting carries. Repeating an identical configuration gives standard deviation of 0.104 in retention ratio. We have not found this quantified for lowrank fine-tuning of language models, and it bounds the reading of every seed-paired comparison in this literature, ours included. 2. Method 2.1. Which form produced which result. The two forms are not interchangeable and the results in this paper do not all come from the same one. The retention experiments on Llama-3-8B (Section 3.2), which are the main claim, use the log-ratio composite of Eq. 4. Earlier structuralpruning experiments on an MLP, not reported here, predate that formulation and use the raw penalty of Eq. 1. We make the mapping explicit because Omega-S otherwise names two objectives, and because one of them is the arm that performs worst on retention. The fix and its cost. Two features of Eq. 2 and Eq. 4 remove the scale sensitivity of the raw form. The logistic maps every entry into [0.5, 1) regardless of the magnitude of , so no longer inherits the scale of the weights at all; and the logarithm makes the gradient proportional to /f rather than to , which removes the remaining dependence on the size of the penalty value. Empirically this is the difference between the weakest arm in the sweep and the strongest (Section 3.2). The map that solved the scale problem is the map that disabled the topological channel. We report both halves of that trade because only one of them was visible when the design was fixed. 2.2. Computational Efficiency For typical transformer dimensions (m = 4096, np = 3), the sequential decomposition yields approximately 79% reduction in computation time relative to the explicit A3 method. The computation is purely structural and requires no gradient graph traversal. When applied to LoRA adapters (rank = 8), the weight matrices are small enough that OmegaS requires zero inter-GPU communication in FSDP environments, as the adapter weights are not sharded. 2.3. Application Frequency We recommend applying Omega-S every [10, 50] steps. The topological impact is cumulative and does not require per-step application. At = 10, amortised overhead is below 4% in all tested configurations.

sections.title: Quick Start
sections.content: Omega-S is designed as drop-in addition to any existing PyTorch training loop. Adding it requires three lines of code: from omega_s import StochasticOmegaS omega = StochasticOmegaS(lambda_omega=0.05, k=10, n_probes=3) # Inside your training loop: loss = model(inputs, labels=inputs).loss loss = loss + omega(model) loss.backward() # add topological penalty every steps For LoRA fine-tuning with HuggingFace + PEFT (recommended): # Works with any PEFT model: zero changes to your existing setup model = get_peft_model(base_model, lora_config) omega = StochasticOmegaS(lambda_omega=0.05, k=10) for step, batch in enumerate(dataloader): loss = model(**batch).loss + omega(model) loss.backward() optimizer.step() Full examples, FSDP integration, and reproduction scripts for all experiments in this paper are available at: https://github.com/BiomeMakers/OmegaS-LLM For commercial licensing or research partnerships: acedo@biomemakers.com 2.4. The design space, and which variant we use Turning the index into training penalty leaves three choices open, and each admits more than one reasonable answer. We enumerate them here and report what each costs, because the choices are not obvious priori and because two of the three turn out not to matter. How the graph is built from the weights. The index is defined on weighted graph and weight matrix is not one, so construction is needed. The default is bounded map on the Gram matrix, = σ(W ). Six alternatives were screened statically on the base weights of the model: the bounded map on the raw matrix, row-wise cosine affinity, rank transform, thresholded graph, doubly stochastic scaling and local scaling. The screen measures the triadic excess C/D, which equals one on graph with no triadic organisation over its density and is therefore an absolute reference that alone does not provide. The default construction returns C/D = 1.0000 to four decimal places in every module tested, equal to its permutation null: the graph it builds carries no triadic content over its density at all. The cosine construction lifts that to median of 1.36 and makes the clustering term move. That looks like the obvious improvement, and it is not: trained on the ten-seed protocol, the cosine composite loses on all ten seeds (0.547 against 0.841, Wilcoxon = 0.002). The 5 ordering is monotone in how much the clustering channel moves, which is the opposite of what topological reading would predict. We keep the default construction and report the negative result in Appendix B.12. Which form of the objective. The index can enter the loss as the raw triadic trace Tr(A3) or as the log-ratio of the four factors, log(M Coex/(C D)). These are not interchangeable and they rank oppositely across our two settings: the composite form wins on retention; in separate experiments on structured pruning, not reported here, the two rank oppositely. We define both explicitly rather than presenting one as the method, and use the composite throughout. How the modularity factor is oriented. enters the denominator of the index, so whether it is taken as modularity measure or as its inverse changes the direction in which the penalty pushes. The ecological observation that motivated the index fixes this: resistant communities show lower modularity, so Ω must decrease with modularity, so must be modularity measure. graph that separates easily into modules has small algebraic connectivity λ2, which makes 1/λ2 the quantity that is large on modular graphs. We therefore take = 1/λ2. We also ran the opposite orientation, = λ2, over the same ten seeds. It gives 76.6% retention against 84.1%, losing on 8 of 10 seeds. The difference, +0.075, is smaller than the run-torun standard deviation of 0.104 we measure in Section 3.4, so the two orientations are not distinguishable from each other at ten seeds; both are distinguishable from the baselines. We report the comparison because of what it says about mechanism rather than about performance: Section 3.3 shows that the modularity term is numerically inert under either orientation, so any difference between them cannot be topological effect of . What inverting the term does change is the scale of the objective, from 1.06 to 10.73 on representative matrix, and since the penalty coefficient is calibrated by gradient ratio, different scale places the one live factor at different operating point. The control is that applying the same inversion under the cosine construction, where the objective does not jump in scale, changes nothing at all: 4 of 10 seeds, mean difference +0.010, = 0.83. What this leaves. Of the three choices, one is settled by the domain the index comes from, one is settled empirically against negative result, and the third is genuine fork with two answers that serve different purposes. The configuration used from here on is: bounded map on the Gram matrix, log-ratio form, = 1/λ2, penalty applied every ten steps with the coefficient calibrated so the penalty gradient is 3% of the task gradient. 3. Experiments 3.1. Experimental Setup Base experiments use three-layer MLP trained on Split-MNIST (digits 04) with architecture [78425612810], Adam optimiser (lr= 103), batch size 128, 5 epochs, seed 42. LLM experiments use Llama-3-8B [15] with LoRA adapters (r=8, α=16). The adapter is inserted into q_proj and v_proj of every attention layer, which is the placement the original LoRA work selects by ablation [9] and the one in near-universal use since; we use it here so that the comparison against baselines that assume it is like for like. Omega-S hyperparameters differ between the two runs, and we give both because the repository quick-start reproduces the first and not the second. The five-seed run of Section B.13 uses fixed λΩ = 0.05 with = 10 and np = 3 probe vectors. The ten-seed run of Section 3.2 uses = 10, np = 16 probes (three was found to give an estimator dominated by sampling noise), sampled subset of eight modules per application, and λΩ calibrated at run time so that the 6 penalty gradient is fixed fraction 0.03 of the task gradient rather than fixed constant; the resulting λΩ therefore varies by seed, between 16 and 41 in this run. 3.2. StabilityPlasticity Trade-off We evaluate Omega-S in sequential fine-tuning setting using Llama-3-8B with LoRA adapters (r=8, α=16), transferring from code (CodeAlpaca-20k [17], 5,000 samples) to prose (Wikitext2 [18], 5,000 samples). Knowledge retention is measured via HumanEval pass@1 [16] (164 problems) evaluated before fine-tuning, after Domain (code), and after Domain (prose). The experiment is replicated with five independent random seeds to assess robustness, with the Omega penalty verified to be connected to the autograd graph before each run. Table 1: Main result (ten-seed experiment) on Llama-3-8B (LoRA, sequential fine-tuning code prose), ten random seeds, penalty connected to the autograd graph, per-arm dedicated RNG. Code kept is absolute HumanEval pass@1 after the prose task and is our primary metric; it is not measure of plasticity, since the second task is prose and HumanEval measures code throughout. Retention is the same quantity divided by post-code HumanEval; values above 1.0 mean net positive transfer on that seed. All arms use the hyperparameters selected in Section B.11; none was re-tuned for this table, which would have given the baselines best-ofseveral advantage that Omega-S did not receive. Every arm in this table was measured in the same session, on the same hardware, so that no comparison mixes the effect with the run-to-run variation quantified in Section 3.4. The wins column counts seeds on which Omega-S keeps more code than that arm, on the absolute measure, and gives the exact sign test and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the paired differences. The corrected orientation is the better of the two, but the paired difference between them, +0.075, is smaller than the run-to-run standard deviation of 0.104 measured in Section 3.4, so the two orientations are not distinguishable from each other on ten seeds. What is distinguishable is each against the baselines, and those comparisons are in Table 1. In the ten-seed experiment, the log-ratio Omega-S improves retention over tuned weight decay on 10 of 10 seeds (mean 61.9% 84.1%, +17.3 pp) and over tuned EWC on 8 of 10 (+17.3 pp), and it does so while ending with the highest absolute code capability of any arm (HumanEval pass@1 = 0.238 after the prose task, against 0.173 with no regulariser). We are careful about what that second number is. It is the numerator of the retention ratio reported in absolute terms, and it is the quantity practitioner cares about, namely how much of the original capability 7 Figure 1: Per-seed retention in the ten-seed experiment, all arms tuned. Omega-S (right bars) exceeds both baselines on most seeds; the two seeds where it trails EWC (123, 3033) are those where EWC itself is highest. The dotted line marks retention = 100% (full retention of the code capability after the prose task). survives. It is not measure of plasticity, and we do not describe it as one: the retention metric is HumanEval throughout while the second task is prose, so nothing in this experiment measures performance on the new task. Whether Omega-S costs plasticity on the second task is untested here and would require Wikitext perplexity measurement we did not make. On the absolute measure Omega-S beats the no-regulariser arm on 9 of 10 seeds (exact sign test, one-sided = 0.011), one more than the 8 of 10 the ratio gives. The discrepancy is instructive. On seed 5055 Omega-S ends with more code capability in absolute terms (0.207 against 0.171) and yet lower retention ratio, because it had also reached higher post-code baseline. The ratio penalises an arm for doing better on the first task, which is the main reason we lead with the absolute figure. The penalty is applied during both tasks, so post-code HumanEval is arm-specific by construction rather than shared baseline; this is why we lead with the absolute metric. The two are nonetheless statistically indistinguishable between the Omega-S and no-regulariser arms: the means are 0.291 against 0.268, Omega-S is ahead on 5 of 10 seeds with one tie (exact sign test, one-sided = 0.50), and the mean paired difference of +0.023 sits well inside its own spread across seeds (sd = 0.050). The retention gain therefore does not arise from different starting point. We ran this experiment after first five-seed run  (Table 8)  that showed the same direction more weakly (4/5 over weight decay); the effect strengthened, rather than regressing to the mean, when we doubled the seeds and tuned every arm on the same footing. This comparison against EWC is worth stating in full, because Omega-S wins it while asking for strictly less. EWC is the standard method for catastrophic forgetting, and to build its penalty it must retain copy of the previous-task weights and estimate Fisher information matrix by passing previous-task data back through the model, so it requires continued access to the old data, which in production is often unavailable (privacy, storage, data that has expired). OmegaS reads only the current weights: no stored optimum, no Fisher matrix, no previous-task data. It therefore beats, on 8 of 10 seeds, the fields standard forgetting baseline while removing that baselines core operational requirement. (We do not claim lower per-step compute: Omega-Ss penalty carries Hutchinson estimate over whose cost we have not benchmarked against 8 EWCs; the advantage we do claim is operational (no dependence on prior data), not raw speed.) The margin is uneven, and its shape suggests ceiling. The per-seed advantage is far from uniform: against the unregularised arm it ranges from 4.4 to +54.3 percentage points. An earlier version of this work read that spread as evidence of two regimes, topological on some weight graphs and closer to norm-balancing on others, set by each seeds initialisation. We tested that directly by measuring the four structural components on every seed (Section 3.3) and it is not supported: on all ten seeds the penalty moves the same component, the variance of node degrees, and the other three do not move at all. We record the two-regime hypothesis as refuted. What the per-seed data do show is simpler. The gain over the unregularised model shrinks as that models own retention rises, with rank correlation of ρ = 0.73 across the ten seeds, and the single seed where Omega-S loses to that baseline (42) is one where the baseline already retains two thirds of its capability. The margin has the shape of ceiling effect: the penalty helps roughly in proportion to how much forgetting there is to prevent. We report this as pattern and not as finding, because at = 10 separating genuine ceiling from regression to the mean would need more seeds than we ran. Not equivalent to norm-balancing. recurring concern for any penalty on is that it may reduce, in practice, to equalising the norms of the weight rows, which would make it reparametrisation of weight decay rather than topological criterion. Table 1 includes the direct control: penalty on the variance of row norms, at the same calibration target, run over the same ten seeds in the same session. It reaches 17.5% retention against 84.1% for Omega-S, losing on all ten seeds (p = 0.002). Row-norm equalisation on its own does not buy retention in this setting. That control is run at Omega-Ss calibration target rather than its own, which is deliberate but debatable choice: it tests whether the same penalty budget spent on norms achieves what spending it on degree variance does. version tuned on its own grid, and protocol defect we found in the original selection, are in Appendix A. 3.3. What the penalty actually moves: direct measurement Omega-S is by mathematical definition topological regulariser: its objective is built from Tr(A3), the third spectral moment of the weight graph = , whose node-wise decomposition carries information no purely spectral index determines (see Method). That is statement about the functional. It leaves open separate, empirical question: under the training conditions of these experiments, which of the objectives components does the penalty actually move to produce the retention gain? We measured this directly rather than assuming it. For each of the ten seeds we trained task twice, once with no regulariser and once with OmegaS, and recorded the four components of the objective (C clustering, density, modularity, Coex degree variance) on the effective LoRA weights, together with the retention gain of that seed. The result is unambiguous and one-sided. The change in clustering is 0 on every seed (e.g. seed 456: moves from 0.999708 to 0.999702), whereas degree variance falls substantially (Coex drops 510%, e.g. seed 456: 201.6 182.8). In other words, the retention effect is carried entirely by the denominators Coex term, not by the numerators clustering term. The reason is structural, not incidental. The pseudo-adjacency is built as = σ(W ), and the logistic σ compresses all entries into [0.5, 1); is therefore close to an all-ones matrix, on which the normalised clustering Tr(A3)/A3 is pinned near its ceiling (C 0.9997) regardless of the underlying weight structure. The clustering channel is saturated and inert by construction: Omega-S cannot raise because σ has already removed the contrast that would let it. What remains free to move is Coex, the variance of node degrees. We name this plainly as design 9 shortcoming rather than technical detail: the logistic map in the construction of is not motivated by the topological objective, and in retrospect it is precisely what disables the clustering channel the method is built to exploit. construction that preserves contrast (Appendix A) would be preferable in any future formulation; we report the saturation here, having measured it, rather than leaving it for reader to infer. How much of the objective is actually live: direct measurement of all four factors. The statement above concerns the clustering term, and reader is entitled to ask what the other three do. We measured the elasticity of each factor with respect to the weights, that is the relative change in the factor produced by relative change in along fixed random direction. The quantity is dimensionless, so it is comparable across factors and modules, and value of zero means the factor cannot contribute gradient at all. Measured on the base weights of Llama-3-8B over ten attention projections spanning layers 0 to 31, each with the branch the implementation actually applies to it: Coex 0.0091 0.0000 Elasticity, base weights Elasticity, trained weights 0.0139 0.0000 Relative change during run 0.00% +0.07% +0.06% 5.87% 0.0000 0.0000 0.0001 0.0001 The three rows measure three different things and agree. The first is the sensitivity of each factor on the models base weights; the second is the same quantity after full fine-tune, which tests whether factor that looks inert at initialisation comes alive once the weights move; the third is the actual change in each factor over run, relative to the unregularised arm, median over the ten seeds. Three of the four factors are numerically inert on all three measures, and one carries everything. Degree variance responds roughly ninety times more strongly than the modularity term, is the only factor above the noise floor, and is the only one that moves during training, falling 5.87% in median while the other three stay under 0.1%. As implemented and in these conditions, the composite objective reduces in practice to penalty on the variance of node degrees. The middle row answers question the first row alone leaves open. If factor looks inert at initialisation, it may still come alive once the weights move, and the two orientations of do differ in outcome (Section 2.4), which would be explained if started contributing during training. It does not: the elasticity of is 0.0001 before and after training alike, and its relative change over run is +0.06%, indistinguishable from the clustering and density terms. Whatever separates the two orientations, it is not the modularity term acting on the weights, which is what leaves the operating-point account of Section 2.4 as the one that fits. The result holds under both orientations of : the numbers above are measured with = 1/λ2, and the degree-variance change under the other orientation was 5 to 10% with the other three factors equally inert. The mechanism does not depend on which of the two is used, which is one more reason to read the difference between them as change of operating point rather than as topological effect. It is worth being precise about what that inertia is property of, because the natural reading is that the frameworks factors are weak and that is not what the measurement says. The bounded map is what flattens them: in the ecological setting from which the index derives, modularity is among the strongest signals available, separating management types with r2 = 0.955 in the survey of soil communities that motivated the construction, comparable to the co-exclusion term and higher than clustering. factor that carries most of the signal in the domain of origin and none under saturating map applied to neural weights is telling us about the map, not about the factor. The same holds for the orientation question above: the direction of is fixed in the 10 framework by that ecological observation and not by convention, and it is only here, where the term does not move, that the orientation ceases to matter. We state the consequence plainly. As currently formulated, and in these conditions, Omega-S operates by reducing the variance of node degrees in the weight graph, quantity that is strongly, though not perfectly, correlated with the variance of weight-row norms (we measure 0.60 here, leaving roughly 40% of degree-variance unexplained by row norms). It is therefore not, in practice, clustering-driven topological method, even though its objective is topological in form. We found no evidence of second, clustering-driven regime: across all ten seeds the movement is dominated by Coex, so the bimodal per-seed pattern of Table 11 is not explained by two structural mechanisms in these data. Three points follow, and we are careful not to overclaim in either direction. First, this does not weaken the empirical result: Omega-S still leaves more code capability than no regularisation on 9/10 seeds (p = 0.011), and leads weight decay on 9/10 and EWC on 8/10 in retention, without access to previous-task data. The methods demonstrated utility stands; only the explanation of why it works is revised, from clustering/topology to degree-variance control. Second, degreevariance control is itself legitimate and, to our knowledge, uncharacterised lever for LoRA continual learning, distinct from generic weight decay; the row-norm control, now swept on its own grid, does not reliably beat no regularisation (6/10) while Omega-S exceeds it on 8/10, which bounds the 40% unexplained component without fully quantifying it. Third, and this is direction we offer to the community rather than result we claim here: the topological channel is inert only because of the saturating σ. reformulation that keeps informative, for instance replacing σ(W ) with contrastpreserving map such as temperature-scaled or rank-normalised affinity, or penalising Tr(A3) on thresholded graph so that clustering is not pinned near 1, would let genuinely clustering-driven variant of Omega-S be tested. Whether such variant outperforms the degree-variance mechanism measured here is untested. We sketch this reformulation in Appendix and leave its evaluation to future work. What the degree sequence measures, and construction detail we must declare. Two further measurements refine the statement above. The first is discrepancy between the text and the reference implementation that we report rather than leave for reader to find. The implementation forms the pseudo-adjacency as σ(W ) only when is non-square; when is square it applies σ(W ) elementwise, without forming the Gram matrix. In Llama-3-8B, q_proj is square and v_proj is not, so the runs reported here used one module of each kind and therefore two constructions at once, while the description above and in the Method section covers only the Gram form. The measured consequence is not cosmetic: on q_proj the degreevariance term differs by factor of roughly 400 between the two branches. This does not affect the reported numbers, which were produced by the code as written, but it does affect how the method should be described, and any reimplementation should fix the branch deliberately in one direction or the other. The second measurement asks what the degree sequence actually encodes, since that is where the entire effect lives. Regressing the degree sequence of the base weights on the row norms and partitioning the variance, the answer differs by branch, and it differs in exactly the way the algebra predicts. Where = σ(W ) and the entries are small, the logistic is close to linear, so the degree of node is essentially the magnitude of its row and column; empirically the row norms explain 96% of the degree variance in layers 8 to 31 of q_proj. Where = σ(W ), the degree is the total absolute alignment of row with all other rows; there the row norms explain only 29% on average across the same layers of v_proj, and the remaining 71% is alignment structure that magnitude does not capture. The regulariser is therefore applying two different criteria depending on module shape: magnitude equalisation on square modules and alignment equalisation on non-square ones. This is consistent with the row-norm control being close to but 11 not equal to Omega-S, and it suggests specific ablation, which we ran. Which channel carries the effect: an ablation by module type. We restricted the penalty to one module type at time while leaving the adapter unchanged on both, so that what varies is which channel is regularised and not where the model can learn. The comparison that matters is between the two ablated arms rather than against the full objective: both concentrate the same calibrated force on half as many modules, so they carry the same bias, whereas comparing either to the full arm would confound channel with intensity. The adapter is unchanged in both arms; only the set of modules the penalty acts on differs. The last row is the reason this comparison must be read with care: the magnitude arm ends the first task with 0.193 HumanEval against 0.289 for the alignment arm, so it learns task substantially worse and its retention ratio is measured against lower denominator. The direction of the difference is the same on the absolute measure, but the magnitude of the gap is not interpretable. Two things follow, and they point in different directions. The alignment channel contributes more: it leads on nine of ten seeds (exact sign test, one-sided = 0.011; Wilcoxon = 9, two-sided = 0.065, which does not clear the threshold because the single loss is also the largest difference), with mean paired advantage of 0.116. But neither channel reproduces the full objective: the alignment arm exceeds it on three seeds of ten and the magnitude arm on two, and the better of the two (0.750) exceeds the no-regularisation baseline (0.631). The effect is not located in one channel; it requires acting on both module types. We also note an observation we cannot yet interpret. The single seed on which the magnitude channel wins, 456, is the one where it wins by the largest margin of any seed in the table, and where it exceeds the full objective (1.148 against 1.023). On seed 5055 the two channels tie and both exceed the full objective. If this pattern held with more seeds it would suggest that different initialisations fall into different regimes, one magnitude-driven and one alignment-driven, which would be candidate explanation for the bimodal per-seed advantage of Table 11 that our earlier structural measurement failed to find. On one seed of ten it is an observation and not finding, and we report it as such. One caveat bounds the whole ablation. Because the calibration fixes the total penalty gradient, restricting to half the modules concentrates that force on half as many, so each ablated arm receives roughly twice the accumulated force per module. This does not affect the comparison between the two ablated arms, which carry the bias equally, but it does affect any comparison against the full objective, and separating channel from intensity there would require further run at reduced target. 12 3.4. How much run-to-run variation this setting carries Every comparison in this paper is paired by seed, which presupposes that the seed identifies the run. We tested that presupposition by repeating an identical configuration: same seed, same code, same hardware, same arm. Four repetitions of one arm and three of another gave standard deviations of 0.068 and 0.104 in retention ratio, with individual pairs as far apart as 0.596 and 0.793. The same held when the four baseline arms were re-measured months after their first run. Three of the four reproduced their means to within 0.04; the per-seed values did not, with standard deviation of 0.104 on the differences. The fourth is worth naming because it changed comparison: EWC, whose mean rose from 0.593 to 0.691 on re-measurement. That is shift of 0.098, the same order as the repeat-to-repeat deviation above, and it moved Omega-S from winning 8 of 10 seeds against EWC on the retention ratio to winning 6. Nothing about either method changed; the earlier EWC measurement simply sat low in its own distribution. This is the concrete reason every arm in Table 1 was measured in single session, and it is what comparison against previously published baseline figure risks. Two consequences follow and we state both. First, the presupposition does not hold in this setting: the seed fixes initialisation and data order but not the non-deterministic reductions in the GPU kernels, so paired test across seeds is comparing runs that differ by more than the seed. Second, any mean difference below roughly 0.066, twice the standard error of ten-seed mean, is not distinguishable here. That bound is what places the two orientations of in the not-distinguishable category while leaving the comparisons against the baselines well outside it. That GPU non-determinism dominates seed-to-seed variance is established elsewhere. Morin and Willetts [25] trained ResNet-50 fifty times with fixed seed and attribute 74 to 87% of the observed standard deviation to it; Nagarajan et al. [26] report 12.4% relative deviation from the same source in reinforcement learning, and Pinto et al. [27] find significant weight and prediction differences between identically configured convolutional runs. We have not found the quantity reported for low-rank fine-tuning of language models, which is the regime here, and we report it because it bounds the reading of every seed-paired comparison in this literature, ours included. The robust design would average several repetitions per cell before pairing; we did not do that, and the cost of doing it is multiplication of the compute budget by the number of repetitions. 3.5. One thing we would like others to run This paper closes with several things untested, listed in Section 3.6. Most need GPU hours and we do not expect anyone to spend them on our behalf. One does not. The mechanism measurement of Section 3.3 runs on base weights and takes minutes. It reports the elasticity of each of the four factors with respect to the weights, and it is what establishes that three of them are inert under the construction used here: python experiments/check_M.py We have run it on one model. The claim that the composite objective reduces in practice to penalty on degree variance is claim about that construction on those weights, and whether it holds elsewhere is the single thing that would most change what this paper can say. report that the factors are live on some other model is as useful to us as one that confirms they are not: it would mean the reduction is specific rather than general, and we would rather know. There is reporting template in the repository. 13 3.6. Limitations The primary limitation is scale: controlled structural experiments (degree variance, FLOPs reduction) were conducted on small MLP with Split-MNIST. The main sequential fine-tuning result (mean retention 61.9% 84.1% over tuned weight decay, ten seeds, 10/10 positive; 8/10 over tuned EWC) is measured on Llama-3-8B with LoRA adapters on public datasets using HumanEval as the retention metric, with the penalty verified connected to the autograd graph. Three caveats bound the interpretation. First, the per-seed advantage is bimodal (large wins, or losses only on the two seeds where EWC itself peaks); ten seeds establish the direction but not per-seed structural model. Second, the mechanism is now measured (Section 3.3): the effect is carried by degree-variance reduction, not clustering, so topological describes the objective, not the operative mechanism in this formulation; how much of the degree-variance effect is separable from row-norm equalisation is now measured rather than assumed. control swept on its own grid does not reliably beat no regularisation (6/10) and Omega-S exceeds it on 8/10, one-sided = 0.055, which does not clear conventional significance at ten seeds. The controls strength was moreover selected on two seeds that proved to be its own worst two, so another strength might serve it better. On GPT-2 (124M, full fine-tuning), connected re-run finds that Omega-S combined with group lasso does not exceed group lasso alone in structured sparsity (0.72% vs. 0.77% FLOPs). We report it because it bounds what the method should be claimed to do: whatever it contributes, it is not compression. The FSDP environment used PCIe rather than NVLink; overhead ratios are valid but should be re-confirmed in higher-bandwidth environment. further limitation concerns what the name Omega-S covers. The retention results use the logratio composite and the pruning results use the raw trace penalty (Section 2.1); these are different objectives on different architectures and tasks, and the raw form is the arm that performs worst on retention. Neither result is invalidated by this, since each was produced by the objective it names, but the two should not be read as evidence for single method until the composite is evaluated on the pruning setting as well. Two further limitations follow from the work reported in Section B.12. The reference implementation builds the pseudo-adjacency as σ(W ) only for non-square and as σ(W ) for square , so the runs reported here mix two constructions, one per module type, while the Method section describes only the first. We report this because it changes how the method should be described and because the degree-variance term differs by roughly factor of 400 between the two branches on q_proj; the numbers themselves are unaffected, having been produced by the code as written. And the negative result on the cosine reformulation is specific to catastrophic forgetting under LoRA on this model and task pair. It does not transfer to the index used as monitoring statistic in domains where the graph is built from correlations rather than from weights, since there the clustering channel is not saturated to begin with and the index is not used to intervene on the network. 4. Conclusion We have introduced Omega-S, graph-based regulariser for large-scale neural networks whose objective is built, via Hutchinson trace estimation, from the clustering coefficient of the weight adjacency matrix . The method is computationally efficient (O(N 2) per layer), adds negligible overhead to training (+1.53.7% at K=10), and requires zero inter-GPU communication in LoRA+FSDP settings. In sequential fine-tuning of Llama-3-8B, the log-ratio form of Omega-S leaves more code capability than no regularisation at all on 9 of 10 seeds (0.173 0.238 absolute HumanEval, +37.7% relative, = 0.011), and leads weight decay on 9 of 10 and EWC on 8 of 10 in retention (61.9% 84.1%), with zero access to previous-domain data. first five-seed run showed the same direction more weakly, so the effect strengthened with sample size. 14 We are explicit about mechanism. Although the objective is topological by construction, direct measurement shows that in this formulation the penalty acts through reduction of node-degree variance, not clustering: the clustering channel is saturated by the logistic map used to build the adjacency and does not move. Omega-S as it stands is thus best understood as degree-variance regulariser with (currently inert) topological objective; whether its benefit is separable from row-norm equalisation is now tested rather than deferred, and control swept on its own grid does not reproduce the gain, though the margin over it does not clear conventional significance at ten seeds. This revises the explanation of the method, not its measured utility, which exceeds both standard baselines. Restoring the topological channel through contrast-preserving construction was the obvious repair and we built it: it does revive the clustering channel and it makes retention worse on all ten seeds (Appendix A). Whether some other construction would do better is open, but the one that seemed most promising priori does not. further limit concerns the scope of the regulariser. Weight decay, used here as retention baseline, is not primarily forgetting method: it is the standard tool for generalisation on single task. Whether Omega-S also competes with weight decay on that ground, that is, whether degree-variance control improves single-task generalisation and not only sequential retention, is coherent follow-up we have not tested and flag without prejudging the outcome. Finally, Omega-S reflects broader principle: structural regularisation principles observed in biological systems can provide productive priors for artificial neural network design. The formalisation of this principle, which runs from soil microbiome network observations [1, 2] to mathematically grounded and empirically validated regulariser for LLMs, represents the central intellectual contribution of this work. Several appendices predate that configuration and report the alternative orientation = λ2. They are: the calibration sweep that selected the penalty strength; the strength sweep of the row-norm control, which is separate experiment from the row-norm arm of Table 1 and asks what that control achieves when tuned on its own grid; the hyperparameter selection protocol for weight decay and EWC; and the cosine construction study. We have not re-run them because what each establishes does not depend on the orientation: the calibration sweep locates target that both configurations use, the row-norm sweep tests whether the effect reduces to norm balancing, and the cosine study asks whether construction that revives the clustering channel helps, which Section 3.3 shows it does not under either orientation. The arms of Table 1 are not among them. No regulariser, weight decay, EWC, the row-norm control and the cosine composite were all re-measured in one session with the configuration this paper uses, using the hyperparameters those earlier sweeps had selected. What was not repeated is the selection of those hyperparameters, not their evaluation. Figures that differ between the two configurations are dated by which appendix they appear in. Where an appendix reports mean retention of 76.6% for Omega-S, that is the alternative orientation; the configuration of this paper gives 84.1%. We say this once here rather than repeating it in each appendix. A. The row-norm control, swept on its own grid This appendix reports the alternative orientation = λ2; see the note above. The row-norm arm of Table 1 is separate and was measured with the configuration of this paper. This is the objection that decides how novel the mechanism is, so we tested it rather than argued about it. Our first attempt at the test failed, and the failure was ours. The tuning phase of the ten-seed run swept weight decay, EWC and the two Omega-S arms; it did not sweep the row-norm control. In the evaluation phase that control was launched with the calibration target selected for OmegaS, value chosen to make different penalty fixed fraction of the task gradient. Two limits bound that reading and we state both. First, at ten seeds the margin of Omega-S over the control does not clear conventional significance; it sits at the same level as the margin over EWC. Second, the controls strength was selected on seeds 42 and 123, which turned out to be its own two worst of the ten (0.453 and 0.509 retention, against 0.583 to 0.914 elsewhere), so its selection is unreliable and another strength might serve it better. We did not re-select on the evaluation seeds, because that would hand the control best-of-several advantage on the evaluation set which Omega-S never had. The effective form is decisive. The raw Tr((W )3) penalty applied directly to LoRA factors (the form used in an earlier iteration of these experiments) is the weakest arm in the same ten-seed sweep (53.9% mean retention, below the 63.1% no-regularisation baseline, winning only 1/10 against weight decay). The log-ratio StochasticOmegaS form is what delivers the results above. We attribute the gap to scale sensitivity of the raw sextic penalty, whose gradient vanishes as weights shrink; the log-ratio form is approximately scale-invariant. Consequently, the library and the experiment scripts are being unified on the log-ratio form, and earlier internal figures that relied on the raw form are superseded. 17 B. Background and Related Work B.1. Topological Properties of Weight Graphs Neural network weight matrices can be interpreted as bipartite graphs where neurons are nodes and weights define edge strengths. When the degree distribution is highly skewed, with small number of neurons capturing most of the total norm, we term these high-degree nodes weight monopolies. The clustering coefficient, proportional to Tr(A3), quantifies the density of local connectivity clusters. We use it as structural descriptor and do not read high value, on its own, as the signature of weight monopoly; as noted above, it is the degree variance that distinguishes distributed from concentrated triadic structure. B.2. Scale-Free Networks in Biological Systems The scale-free network model [12] describes graphs where the degree distribution follows power law (k) kγ. Such networks exhibit high resilience to random node failures while remaining vulnerable to targeted attacks on hubs. Studies by Biome Makers and collaborators have characterised the topological structure of microbial interaction networks across diverse agricultural conditions. Ortiz-Álvarez et al. [1] demonstrated that farming practices in vineyard soils produce measurable disturbances in the network properties of local fungal communities, with structural monopolies emerging under high anthropogenic pressure. At global scale, Saati-Santamaría et al. [2] showed that soil microbial diversity and network organisation respond consistently to land use and agricultural inputs worldwide, establishing degree distribution and hub structure as reliable indicators of ecosystem health across biomes. These topological properties are further formalised as diagnostic tools in two Biome Makers patents: one on evaluating ecological disturbance via network properties of organism communities [4], and one that defines resilience indices derived from the transitivity of bacterial and fungal co-occurrence networks [3]. The latter is the direct antecedent of the present work. One qualification is needed for accuracy: the global transitivity of graph is proportional to Tr(A3), whereas the vineyard study computes the average of the local transitivities, which captures the same triadic closure but is different functional and is not proportional to Tr(A3). The lineage runs through the notion of triadic closure, not through an identity of statistics. B.3. Hutchinson Trace Estimator The Hutchinson estimator provides an unbiased stochastic approximation of the trace of matrix : Tr(M ) 1 n (cid:88) i=1 M zi, zi Rademacher(1). Related Regularisation Methods Weight Decay / L2 pushes all weights uniformly toward zero, agnostic to structural role. As we show empirically, it produces unstructured sparsity not amenable to FLOPs reduction via structural pruning. 18 SAM [5] seeks flat minima in the loss landscape and is blind to the internal topology of weight matrices. Omega-S and SAM are complementary, not competing. Graph-spectral regularisers. Fiedler regularisation [6] penalises the algebraic connectivity λ2 of the graph induced by during training, with theoretical support from spectral graph theory and an equivalent formulation as structurally weighted L1 penalty. It is the closest antecedent to the present work in kind: functional of graph built from the weights, minimised as part of the training objective rather than computed as diagnostic. Two things separate the two. First, the objective here is triadic, built on Tr(A3), and λ2 appears only as one of four factors; graph-theoretic penalty defined on bipartite construction, as several in this family are, would annihilate the triadic term identically. Second, and against our own interest, our measurement (Section 3.3) finds the λ2 channel numerically inert in this construction, so we make no claim to improve on Fiedler regularisation on its own ground; the comparison remains to be run. Structured / Group Sparsity [11] explicitly targets neuron elimination based on weight magnitude. In our own measurements the composite penalty combined with group lasso does not exceed group lasso alone in the compression achieved, which is why we make no claim in that direction here. B.5. Geometric and Spectral Approaches to Continual Learning parallel and rapidly developing line of work attacks catastrophic forgetting by reasoning about the geometry of weight matrices rather than the magnitude of individual parameters. MuonOGD [22] argues that Frobenius-norm geometry is not the natural choice for matrix-valued LLM parameters, and reformulates projection-based continual learning under spectral-norm geometry, reporting gains on the standard and 15-task continual-learning benchmarks and on TRACE [36]. Related efforts constrain the spectral norm and stable rank of routing manifolds in mixtureof-experts architectures [23], or penalise functional drift within the top-k eigenspace of task kernel [24]. Our premise, that the topology of weight matrix and not merely the size of its entries governs how new learning overwrites old, is shared by this literature and independently supported by it. geometric law for forgetting, and measurement of ours that speaks to it. Steele [28] gives geometric account of forgetting in LoRA specifically, reporting that it follows = α(1 cos2 θmin) + β, where θmin is the minimum principal angle between the task gradient subspaces, validated on synthetic tasks, Split-CIFAR100 with ViT-LoRA and sequential GLUE with RoBERTa-LoRA. Two consequences of that law bear on the present work. The first is that we can report measurement of the governing quantity on model of the scale evaluated here. In separate screen we computed the principal angles between the row spaces of two rank-8 LoRA deltas trained on different tasks from common Llama-3-8B backbone, across all sixty-four attention projections. Against simulated null for two random eight-dimensional subspaces in R4096 (leading cosine 0.077 on average, 0.100 at the maximum over three hundred draws), the leading principal cosine is 3 to 5 times the null in fifty of the sixty-four modules, while the second and all subsequent angles are indistinguishable from it. The overlap between two adapters trained on different tasks is therefore essentially rank one: they share one direction, and the rest of their agreement is chance. It also varies systematically with depth, being largest in the first and last layers and smallest in the middle, and five modules sit exactly at the null. The second is positioning point. Steele reports that orthogonalisation methods such as O-LoRA add little when natural orthogonality is already high. In our measurement seven of the eight directions are at the null, that is already near-orthogonal, so on that reading an orthogonalisation approach would have limited room in this setting. Omega-S does not orthogonalise; it acts on the degree distribution of the weight graph, which is different quantity, and this is one reason 19 the two families are complementary rather than competing. An objection from function space, which we record rather than answer. Hidekel and Raviv [24] argue in the NTK regime that forgetting concentrates in small number of old-task kernel eigenmodes, and that this explains why regulariser acting in parameter space can miss interference in output space. Omega-S is parameter-space regulariser, so the objection applies to it directly and we state it rather than passing over it. Two things bound it in our setting without dissolving it. Their claim is that parameter-space methods can miss such interference, not that they cannot help: the retention results reported here are obtained by parameter-space penalty and hold on nine of ten seeds. And their account predicts where ceiling should lie, which is testable statement about our method that we have not tested. Measuring whether the residual forgetting under Omega-S concentrates in the old-task kernel eigenmodes their theory identifies would establish whether the two accounts describe the same limit, and we identify it as an experiment we have not run. sharper version of the same objection, and what separates our method from its target. Ning et al. [29] make the empirical case that weight-space regularisation underperforms on large language models because the models are polysemantic: per-weight importance estimates of the kind EWC computes are too coarse to isolate the knowledge that needs protecting. They report that task-relevant representations are linearly separable in sparse-autoencoder feature basis but indistinguishable from chance in the weight basis, and that weight-space protection is close to non-selective at the concept level, and they regularise in activation space instead. This is the most direct challenge to the family Omega-S belongs to that we are aware of, and we would rather engage it than omit it. The engagement is distinction, not rebuttal. Non-Uniform Structured Pruning of LLMs growing body of work demonstrates that uniform sparsity across transformer layers is suboptimal [14], motivating non-uniform sparsity allocation strategies that assign differentiated pruning budgets per layer. OWL [14] allocates higher sparsity to layers with fewer activation outliers, mapping the outlier distribution linearly to sparsity ratios. It demonstrates consistent improvements over uniform Wanda and SparseGPT at high sparsity levels. AlphaPruning [37] estimates per-layer importance using Random Matrix Theory, specifically the heavy-tailed spectral exponent of the weight matrix. Layers with heavier-tailed spectra are considered more important and receive lower sparsity. This is the closest prior work to Omega-S in spirit: both use structural property of the weight matrix (rather than activation statistics) to guide pruning. SV-NUP [38] quantifies per-layer contribution via Shapley values, enabling tailored pruning budgets that preserve the most critical layers. Notably, [38] also cites topological insights into restricted Boltzmann machines [40] as motivation, the same class of structural observations that underlies Omega-S. DarwinLM [39] uses evolutionary search to discover optimal non-uniform sparsity allocations, trading off computation for accuracy. Distinction from Omega-S. These methods share with Omega-S the premise that weightmatrix structure carries actionable information, but they differ in stage, objective, and quantity. OWL and AlphaPruning operate after training as allocators of compression budget; their target is inference efficiency at fixed accuracy. Omega-S instead acts during training as regulariser on the topology of each weight matrix, and its target is knowledge retention, that is, resistance 21 to catastrophic forgetting under sequential fine-tuning, rather than compression. Where AlphaPruning measures the heavy-tailedness of layers spectrum to decide how much to prune, Omega-S reshapes the weight-graph structure during optimisation to reduce its concentration (degree variance). The two directions are therefore complementary rather than competing: model regularised with Omega-S can still be pruned afterward by OWL or AlphaPruning, and the questions they answer, namely how much of each layer to remove versus how to train weights that forget less, do not overlap. We do not claim Omega-S as pruning-allocation signal; its contribution is at training time, on retention. B.7. Conceptual Origin: From Soil Microbiomes to Neural Networks The conceptual origin of Omega-S lies not in the loss landscape geometry of deep learning, but in the observed topological properties of biological information networks, specifically the connectivity structure of microbial communities in agricultural soil ecosystems. Empirical studies of soil microbiome networks report that agricultural disturbance systematically reorganises the association structure of the community. In survey of 350 vineyard soils across two countries [1], soils under low-intervention management showed higher clustering coefficient, lower modularity and lower proportion of co-exclusion edges than conventionally managed soils, combination the authors read as denser, less niche-partitioned communities with greater resistance to species loss. In global survey of 1,921 soils from 33 countries [2], agricultural inputs consistently reduced network density across both bacterial and fungal communities, which the authors associate with reduced functional redundancy. We are deliberate about what we do and do not take from this. The two studies use different association estimators, different units of analysis (one network per sample against one network per condition) and different clustering definitions, so their individual factors are not directly comparable and we do not pool them into single directional claim. Neither reports degree distributions or power-law fits, so we make no scale-free claim here; an earlier version of this paper did, and it was not supported by the sources cited. What the two share is that disturbance reorganises network structure in directions their authors link to lower resilience. The intuition we carry across is accordingly weak one: how connectivity is distributed over network, and not only how much of it there is, carries information about robustness that node counts and diversity indices do not. This biological observation raises compelling question for artificial neural networks: do similar structural monopolies emerge during training, and if so, do they carry analogous costs in terms of robustness, generalisation, and efficiency? The answer, we argue, is yes. During the training of large language models, small subset of neurons progressively concentrates disproportionate weight connectivity across layers, creating highly non-uniform degree distributions in the implicit weight graph. This concentration, which we term weight monopolies, persists even under strong weight decay and sharpness-aware optimisation, which target the loss landscape geometry but leave the internal topology of weight matrices untouched. B.8. Thermodynamic and Information-Theoretic Framing The connection between biological network topology and artificial neural networks has deeper thermodynamic grounding. In physical systems, the principle of minimum energy dissipation (related to Boltzmanns entropy formulation) predicts that stable, efficient systems minimise redundant energy flows by distributing load across available channels. Structural monopolies represent thermodynamically inefficient configurations: they concentrate functional load on subset of nodes while leaving the remaining capacity idle. 22 The clustering coefficient of network, quantified as the normalised count of closed triangles in the connectivity graph and proportional to Tr(A3), is sensitive measure of how triadic structure is distributed. We deliberately do not attach direction to it. The same triangle count is compatible with connectivity spread evenly across the graph and with connectivity concentrated on hub and its core, and what separates those two configurations is the variance of the node degrees rather than the triangle count itself (Section 3.3 and [21]). What we retain here is only that Tr(A3) is structural quantity distinct from parameter magnitude, and that its gradient is cheap enough to apply during training. This framing connects Omega-S to broader principle: just as the curvature of spacetime governs the trajectories of physical systems in general relativity, the topological curvature of the weight connectivity graph governs the flow of information through neural network. Standard regularisers operate on the metric of the loss landscape; Omega-S operates on the metric of the networks internal topology. B.9. Weight decay was swept over {0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1}; the grid included zero, so the procedure was free to switch the regulariser off, and it did not, returning λ = 0.05. B.17. Biological Analogy and Its Limits The microbial network analogy is productive but imperfect. Biological scale-free networks emerge from evolutionary pressure over millions of generations; neural weight graphs emerge from gradient descent over thousands of steps. The analogy provides structural intuition, not mathematical equivalence: systems that process and route information efficiently tend to avoid extreme connectivity concentration. The empirical validation of this intuition constitutes the contribution of this paper; the biological framing provides motivation and vocabulary, while the mathematical and empirical results stand independently. B.18. Broader Applications Beyond structural pruning and sequential fine-tuning, Omega-S opens several promising research directions. In model quantisation, weight monopolies often correlate with activation outliers, primary bottleneck for sub-8-bit post-training quantisation that motivates outlier-handling mechanisms such as LLM.int8() [19] and SmoothQuant [20]. By redistributing weight density, Omega-S might yield networks that are inherently more quantisation-friendly. We flag this as hypothesis rather than finding: in preliminary probing at small scale we observed the expected reduction in degree variance but no corresponding improvement in post-quantisation accuracy, with weight decay performing comparably or better. Whether the effect appears at LLM scale, where outlier structure is far more pronounced, remains open. In Federated Learning, applying unified topological prior across decentralised nodes could mitigate structural divergence of local models trained on heterogeneous data, potentially improving weight aggregation stability. The absence of inter-GPU communication cost demonstrated in Section 4.5 suggests negligible overhead even in bandwidth-constrained settings. In Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures, the framework could penalise routing monopolies, preventing expert collapse and ensuring more balanced token-to-expert assignment distribution. The formulation extends beyond artificial neural networks. In computational biology, applying Omega-S constraints to graph neural networks predicting biological pathways could yield representations better aligned with the natural robustness of living systems. In quantitative finance, the penalty could regularise financial ML models to inherently penalise over-reliance on clustered economic nodes, yielding more robust portfolio optimisation and risk forecasting. These interdisciplinary applications underscore the fundamental nature of topological regularisation across any domain where network structure dictates system resilience, principle observed in global soil microbiomes [1, 2, 4] long before it was formalised in the context of artificial neural networks. A. contrast-preserving reformulation of the clustering term Section 3.3 showed that, as implemented, the clustering channel is inert: the pseudo-adjacency = σ(W ) compresses all affinities into [0.5, 1), so is near an all-ones matrix and the normalised clustering Tr(A3)/A3 sits at its ceiling ( 0.9997) irrespective of weight structure. The penalty can therefore only act through the degree-variance term Coex. This appendix sketches how to restore an informative clustering channel, so that genuinely clustering-driven variant of Omega-S can be tested. We present it as an open direction for the community, not as result of this paper. The problem is the saturating map, not Tr(A3) itself. Any of the following keeps responsive to structure: (i) Temperature-scaled affinity. Replace = σ(W ) with Aτ = σ(cid:0)W /τ b(cid:1), choosing the temperature τ and bias so that the affinities span usable range of [0, 1] rather than collapsing to [0.5, 1). Concretely, set to the median of /τ so that roughly half the entries fall below 0.5; then Aτ has genuine contrast and Tr(A3 τ ) varies with the actual triadic structure. The objective and its Hutchinson estimator are otherwise unchanged. (ii) Thresholded graph. Form sparse graph Aθ = 1{W > θ} (or smooth surrogate σ(κ(W θ)) with large κ), with θ per-layer quantile of . Clustering on thresholded graph is the standard network-science definition and is not pinned near 1; its third moment then measures true triadic closure. The trade-off is that the hard threshold must be relaxed (via the smooth surrogate) to keep the penalty differentiable. (iii) Rank-normalised affinity. Map through its empirical CDF so that is uniform on [0, 1] by construction. This removes scale and saturation effects entirely and makes depend only on the ordering of affinities, i.e. on graph topology rather than magnitude. Under any of these, one can define clustering-only arm and degree-variance-only arm (the rownorm / Coex control of the main text, re-tuned to remain functional learner). One point must be settled before such an arm is run, and we flag it rather than resolve it: nothing measured here determines the sign of the clustering term. The objective as implemented minimises Tr(A3); the resilience index from which it derives [21] carries the clustering coefficient in its numerator and therefore rewards raising it; and the measurement of Section 3.3 does not arbitrate between the two, because did not move at all. clustering-only arm should accordingly test both directions, penalising + Tr(A3)/A3 , rather than assuming one. An earlier draft of this appendix specified only the second, which was an unexamined inheritance from the index rather than considered choice. Running both, plus full Omega-S, on the ten-seed protocol would decompose the retention gain into clustering component and degree-variance component, and would settle whether the topological channel (inert here only because of σ) contributes once it is allowed to. We conjectured, in an earlier version of this appendix, that contrast-preserving would add retention on the seeds where the weight graph departs most from degree-only description (the 40% of degree variance not captured by row norms). and Tr(A3)/A3 Outcome. That experiment has since been run and the conjecture does not hold. Section B.12 reports it in full: row-wise cosine affinity removes the saturation, makes the clustering channel steerable during training, and then loses to the original formulation on all ten seeds (p = 0.002), with clustering-only arm worse still. We leave this appendix in place because the diagnosis it 33 contains is correct and because the reasoning that led to the reformulation is what made the test possible; the conjecture at its close is what the evidence overturns.
